sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models are rapidly scaling toward longer contexts, with context windows expanding from 2K tokens to 128K and beyond [Grattafiori et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2024]. As sequence lengths grow, the attention mechanism [Vaswani et al., 2017] becomes central efficiency bottleneck in both inference and training. During inference, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length, consuming substantial GPU memory and constraining both serving concurrency and generation latency. During training and prefill, the FLOPs of attention computation scale quadratically with sequence length. Since the design of the attention mechanism jointly determines KV cache size, computational cost, and model expressiveness, it is critical factor governing the overall efficiency and quality of large language models. Equal contribution. Work done at Baidu Inc. Corresponding author. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). The design of existing attention mechanisms faces three mutually constraining objectives, forming an impossible triangle: KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. Consider the widely adopted Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) [Ainslie et al., 2023]: GQA with 8 KV heads (GQA8) achieves strong quality, but incurs KV cache of 4 KB per layer per token (in BF16). Directly reducing the number of KV heads to 2 (GQA-2) compresses the cache to 1 KB, but dramatically enlarges the group size so that far more query heads must share the same key-value pairs, causing attention diversity to drop sharply and resulting in 1.00% quality degradation at the 1.7B scale. Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) [Liu et al., 2024] applies low-rank compression to reduce KV cache to 1.12 KB, but yields the lowest quality across multiple model scales. Multi-matrix Factorization Attention (MFA) [Hu et al., 2025] reduces the cache to 1 KB by enlarging the head dimension, achieving quality close to GQA-8, but at the cost of 49.8% increase in training and prefill FLOPs (1.7B, S=4096). No existing approach achieves satisfactory balance across all three dimensions. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices of the impossible triangle through two lightweight linear operations. The core idea of VHA is to halve the number of physical query heads while setting the number of KV heads to only 2. Premix then applies near-identity linear transformation to queries within each KV group, expanding the reduced physical query heads into virtual query heads to recover attention diversity. Linear Postmix applies low-rank identity-residual transformation (I + AB, r=H q/2, e.g., r=4 at 1.7B) on the attention output, fusing cross-group inter-head features. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be directly folded into the query projection matrix and Postmix into the output projection matrix at inference time, reducing the model to standard GQA-2 architecture that reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations in mainstream serving frameworks such as vLLM [Kwon et al., 2023] and SGLang [Zheng et al., 2024]. Moreover, with only 2 KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during the decoding phase. Across four model scales (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B dense, and 8B-A1B MoE) with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale (+0.05% to +0.81%), while reducing KV cache by 4 vs. GQA-8 at dense scales and 2 vs. GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9% (1.7B, S=4096). On an industrial 30BA3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by +0.70 / +2.60 % on 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite, demonstrating scalability to industrial model scale. separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison further extends this advantage to 128K context under more aggressive KV compression. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. We propose VHA, employing Premix and Linear Postmix, two lightweight linear operations that simultaneously reduce KV cache and training/prefill FLOPs while improving model quality. 2. VHA uses only linear operations and can be fully absorbed into standard GQA-2 model at inference time, reusing existing serving frameworks such as vLLM and SGLang with zero additional overhead. 3. Direct inspection of the trained Premix and Postmix matrices reveals two complementary structures (group-conditioned query specialization and structured low-rank cross-head communication) that jointly close the gap of the doubly-compressed configuration; component ablations confirm that neither module is sufficient on its own. 4. Comprehensive evaluations across five scales (0.6B to 30B-A3B MoE) against MHA, GQA, MFA, and MLA establish VHA as the best attention mechanism that is Pareto-optimal on KV cache, training/prefill FLOPs, and downstream quality simultaneously; matched long-context evaluations through 128K further validate this advantage under aggressive KV compression.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 KV Cache Efficient Attention Standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) [Vaswani et al., 2017] maintains independent key and value projections per head, causing the KV cache to grow linearly with the number of heads. Multi-Query Attention (MQA) [Shazeer, 2019] shares single KV head across all query heads, drastically reducing the cache at the cost of quality. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) [Ainslie et al., 2023] interpolates 2 between MHA and MQA by allowing multiple query heads to share group of KV heads, and has been widely adopted in LLaMA 2/3 [Touvron et al., 2023, Grattafiori et al., 2024] and Qwen2 [Yang et al., 2024]. Several recent designs further compress the KV cache. Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) [Liu et al., 2024] projects KV into shared low-rank latent space and absorbs the up-projection matrices into and at inference, but requires custom kernels and non-standard inference pipeline. Multi-matrix Factorization Attention (MFA) [Hu et al., 2025] enlarges the head dimension while reducing the number of KV heads, preserving model capacity under tight cache budget but substantially increasing training and prefill FLOPs. Tensor Product Attention (TPA) [Zhang et al., 2025] decomposes QKV into context-dependent tensor products. Grouped-head Latent Attention (GTA) [Sun et al., 2025] extends MLAs global latent space to group-wise design. Simulated Attention Score (SAS) [Zheng et al., 2025] projects small number of low-dimensional KV heads into higher-dimensional spaces to simulate more attention heads, an idea related to VHAs virtual head expansion; however, SAS operates on the KV side whereas VHA virtualizes on the query side. Low-Rank Key-Value Attention (LRKV) [ONeill et al., 2026] shares full-rank KV basis across heads and restores head-specific flexibility through low-rank residuals, form reminiscent of VHAs Postmix (I + AB); yet LRKV acts in KV space and its additional structure remains at inference time. Cross-Layer Attention (CLA) [Brandon et al., 2024] and YOCO [Sun et al., 2024] reduce memory by sharing or reusing KV caches across layers. Unlike all of the above, VHA employs richer training-time parameterization that merges exactly back into standard GQA at deployment, requiring no custom kernels or specialized inference procedures. 2.2 Inter-Head Communication and Virtual Heads Talking-Heads Attention [Shazeer et al., 2020] applies learned linear projections across heads before and after softmax, pioneering inter-head communication. Cordonnier et al. [2020] analyze multi-head attention from collaborative perspective, revealing substantial redundancy among heads. More recently, Explicit Multi-head Attention (MEA) [Peng et al., 2026] introduces head-level linear composition module for explicit cross-head interaction, and Interleaved Head Attention [Duvvuri et al., 2026] interleaves head representations to enable information exchange. In contrast to these methods, VHA does not mix across heads in the attention weight space; instead, it virtualizes in the query space via Premix and fuses inter-head features in the output space via low-rank Postmix, with all operations being strictly linear and fully absorbable at inference. 2.3 Reparameterization RepVGG [Ding et al., 2021] uses multi-branch training architecture (33 + 11 + identity) that merges into single convolution at inference, demonstrating that decoupled training-time parameterization provides implicit regularization at zero inference cost. LoRA [Hu et al., 2022] performs parameter-efficient fine-tuning via low-rank decomposition (W + BA). VHA extends this reparameterization paradigm from single weight matrix to the head dimension of attention: Premix structurally factorizes the per-virtual-head query projections ((cid:102)W (i,g) premix ), while Postmix introduces low-rank identity-residual mixing on the head axis (I + AB). Both modules are mathematically equivalent in the forward pass to standard GQA configuration, yet the decoupled parameterization yields distinct optimization dynamics during training and merges back into standard GQA-2 architecture at inference with zero overhead. = (i) Q

sections.title: 5 Analysis: How VHA Reparameterization Works
sections.content: Beyond task accuracy, VHA should exploit the limited information available under aggressive KV sharing. We therefore inspect the Premix and Postmix matrices of trained VHA models (Premix on the 1.7B, Postmix on the 4B model), asking whether (i) Premix learns group-conditioned query geometry, (ii) Postmix learns structured low-rank cross-head communication, and (iii) the two jointly close the doubly-compressed gap of Section 4.4. Premix learns non-trivial, group-differentiated query transforms. Premix introduces learnable per-group query transform premix before RoPE, initialized near identity. Two trivial outcomes would falsify our hypothesis: (a) premix remains near identity after training, rendering the module no-op; or (b) all KV groups converge to the same matrix, degenerating Premix into group-agnostic shared adapter without group-conditioned specialization. Figure 2 refutes both: panel (a) shows that premix IF is substantially nonzero and most pronounced in mid-to-late layers (peak 5.85), and panel (b) shows that the inter-group distance premix is of comparable 2 value expected under fully independent magnitude (peak 6.13), yielding ratio well below the groups and far above the zero expected under shared deviation. This quantifies that the two KV groups learn substantially but not independently different query transforms. Premix therefore learns differentiated query probing directions per KV group under fixed minimal KV cache, realizing genuine group-conditioned virtual-head expansion rather than mere parameter augmentation. premix g2 g1 Postmix learns structured low-rank cross-head communication. Postmix recombines the Hv attention output heads via the low-rank residual + BA, where entry (j, i) of AB encodes the contribution of source head to recombined head i. The central question is whether AB merely performs per-head rescaling (a strictly diagonal pattern) or genuinely redistributes information across heads (off-diagonal flow). Figure 3 visualizes AB for the trained 4B model and reveals pronounced off-diagonal flow, ruling out the trivial per-head-rescaling outcome. The dominant 9 pattern is within-group redistribution: Postmix primarily rebalances information among heads sharing the same KV cache, with sparse but consistent set of cross-group bridges providing inter-group connectivity without additional KV heads. Joint reparameterization closes the doubly-compressed gap. Tying these analyses back to the component ablation in Table 4 clarifies the three numbers reported there. Premix-only retains the group-conditioned query geometry of Figure 2 but lacks Postmixs cross-group repair pathway, hence the 0.78% gap at 1.7B. Postmix-only owns the cross-head mixing channels of Figure 3 but operates over collapsed, unspecialized virtual heads, hence the 0.14% gap. Only the joint configuration realizes both structures simultaneously, yielding +0.41% advantage over GQA-8 at 25% of its KV cache. VHAs effectiveness therefore arises from the functional complementarity of its two modules: Premix and Postmix are not interchangeable, and neither suffices alone.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We have presented Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which mitigates the tension among KV cache size, training/prefill FLOPs, and model quality through two lightweight linear operations: Premix and Linear Postmix. By halving physical query heads and recovering expressiveness via virtual head expansion and low-rank cross-group mixing, VHA reduces the KV cache to its architectural minimum while simultaneously lowering training FLOPs and improving model quality. Since all added operations are strictly linear, VHA fully absorbs into standard GQA-2 at inference, reusing existing serving optimizations with zero additional overhead. Analysis of trained models reveals that Premix and Postmix are functionally complementary and neither suffices alone, explaining why the joint configuration consistently surpasses the GQA baseline across all five evaluated scales (0.6B to 30B-A3B MoE). matched 10B-A1B evaluation further shows that VHA maintains this advantage over GQA through 128K context.

sections.title: Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Our largest validation is at the 30B-A3B MoE scale trained on 500B tokens; scaling VHA to larger MoE models and substantially more training data (e.g., 20T tokens) remains an important direction. We further validate VHA through 128K on 10B-A1B MoE, while broader long-context architectures and training recipes remain to be explored. VHAs behavior under reinforcement learning training paradigms is also worth exploring. Finally, VHA is orthogonal to other KV cache compression techniques such as quantization and sparsification, and combining them may yield further inference savings. Long-Context Evaluation A.1 Model and Stage-wise Training We conduct controlled long-context comparison on MiMo-2.5-Flash-style 10B-A1B MoE backbone that interleaves full and sliding-window attention at 1:3 ratio. The GQA and VHA models share the same backbone, data, optimization settings, and sliding-window layers. They differ only in the full-attention layers: GQA uses four KV heads, whereas VHA uses two; all sliding-window layers use eight KV heads in both models. Thus, VHA halves the KV cache of the full-attention layers without changing the sliding-window component. The 8K pretraining stage uses 500B tokens and ends at 60K steps. Long-context mid-training then uses 100B tokens at 32K followed by another 100B tokens at 128K. These stages add 12K and 24K steps, yielding cumulative checkpoints at 72K and 96K steps, respectively. The RoPE base is increased from 104 at 8K to 6.4105 at 32K and 5106 at 128K. We report intermediate results from the 32K checkpoint and final results from the 128K checkpoint. A.2 RULER and HELMET We evaluate RULER and HELMET from 8K to 128K. RULER Overall is the mean over 13 tasks: eight Retrieval, two Aggregation, two QA, and one Variable Tracking task. HELMET is reported by category because its categories measure distinct capabilities. At the final checkpoint, VHA leads RULER Overall at every evaluated length, with an average of 84.4 across lengths versus 73.0 for GQA. The largest gap occurs in Variable Tracking, where VHA scores 92.6/87.2/83.0 at 32K/64K/128K versus 3.2/4.2/3.0 for GQA. HELMET is more heterogeneous: averaged across lengths, VHA wins RAG, LongQA, and Summarization, ties Reranking, and trails on ICL. A.3 Complementary Long-Context Evaluations We additionally report LongBench-v2, InfiniteBench, BABILong, short-context eight-task average, and language-modeling bits per byte on the four ProLong domains. At the final checkpoint, VHA wins seven of the eight reported metrics; InfiniteBench is nearly tied.

Despite this redundancy, the separated parameterization {WO, A, B} provides training advantages analogous to those observed in RepVGG [Ding et al., 2021]: 1. Factored gradient paths. The gradients with respect to A, B, and WO follow different paths through the computation graph. This factorization provides form of implicit regularization, as the effective weight update to at each step is constrained by the low-rank structure of AB. 2. Identity initialization. With initialized to zero, BA = 0 and = at the start of training. Postmix begins as no-op and gradually learns useful cross-group mixing patterns, avoiding disruption to the early training dynamics. 3. Low-rank constraint. The bottleneck rank Hv limits the expressiveness of the cross-head mixing, acting as structural regularizer. This prevents Postmix from overfitting, consistent with the ablation finding that larger ranks (r=32, 128) degrade evaluation performance despite lower training loss.
